passage: Vikas waited until the Monday meeting room emptied. "Deepak, do you have five minutes about the weekend rota?" Deepak glanced at the clock but nodded. Vikas slid over a one-page table: weekend hours for each team over the last two months, his own team's column clearly the longest. "I think this got uneven without anyone meaning it," he said. "Could we rotate it, so each team takes every third weekend?" Deepak frowned at the numbers, tapped his pen and said he'd think about it. Walking back to his desk, Vikas noted the date and the conversation in his own log. It was unfair, but nobody was at risk and nothing dishonest was going on, so going over Deepak's head was not something he wanted to spend on this.

qa.q: What did Vikas bring to Deepak in the meeting room?
qa.a: A one-page table of weekend hours for each team over two months, with a suggestion to rotate the weekends.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel about the rota, and why did he not go over Deepak's head?
qa.a: Vikas was frustrated because the rota was unfair, but he saw no danger and nothing dishonest, so he decided escalating was not worth it.

qa.q: What could Vikas do if Deepak does not change the rota?
qa.a: Follow up after a week with the same numbers, ask what would make a rotation workable, and escalate only if a real safety or ethics issue appears.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Vikas's table?
qa.a: Deepak might feel a little challenged, but since it came privately with a workable alternative, it may feel more like help than an accusation.

grounding: Shows an employee documenting a concern, offering an alternative and choosing not to escalate a non-ethical unfairness.

passage:
Thursday night. Lalremsiami, my manager, backed me when the audit went badly last year, and I haven't forgotten. Today Lalremsiami said, "Just tell the client the shipment is on track." It isn't. The truck is stuck for at least a week. My stomach turned. I owe Lalremsiami a lot, but I can't tell a customer something false when they're planning around it. Loyalty can't mean that. So I said, "I'll give them the real date and offer a partial shipment. I'd rather you hear it from me now than find out later." Lalremsiami went quiet, then said, "Send it tomorrow." Not happy, not angry either. I'm shaky but sure.

Damini

qa.q: Why does Damini feel indebted to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Lalremsiami backed Damini when the audit went badly last year.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when refusing to say the shipment was on track?
qa.a: Damini felt torn between gratitude and conscience: Damini's stomach turned, and Damini ends up shaky but sure.

qa.q: How did Damini stay honest without blindsiding the manager?
qa.a: Damini told Lalremsiami first, offered a partial shipment as a fix, and said the client would get the real date.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt hearing Damini's answer?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may have felt pressure over losing the client and some discomfort at being contradicted, though the quiet reply suggests they accepted the plan. 🤔

grounding: Shows an employee weighing loyalty to a manager against honesty to a customer and choosing honesty while staying respectful.

passage: Session note, Tuesday. Karthik arrived shaking with anger. Sabina, his partner in their small design studio, had moved the two biggest clients to her own new firm without telling him. He said he wanted to post everything about her online and "make sure nobody hires her again." I asked him to hold that thought for a day and not send anything tonight. We listed what he could do instead: gather the emails and contracts in one folder, read the partnership agreement, and book a consultation with a lawyer. He stopped pacing about halfway through. Before leaving he said, "I can be furious and still not do something I'll regret." I will check in on Friday to see whether the folder exists.

qa.q: What had Sabina done to make Karthik so angry?
qa.a: Sabina had moved the two biggest clients to her own new firm without telling him.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling and wanting at the start of the session?
qa.a: He felt furious and wanted to expose Sabina online so nobody would hire her again.

qa.q: What calm steps did the narrator suggest to protect Karthik and his work?
qa.a: Gather the emails and contracts in one folder, read the partnership agreement and book a consultation with a lawyer.

qa.q: What would change for Karthik's own studio if he had posted the attacks that night?
qa.a: His time and attention would likely go into the fight instead of the work and the clients he still has, and it could weaken his position.

grounding: Shows a business owner raging at a partner's betrayal and considering revenge, guided towards calm, documented steps.

passage:
Vishal,

Here are the terms as I understand them. You keep the delivery van and the wholesale accounts. I keep the shop lease and the recipes. We settle the books by the end of the month, with both of us signing the final sheet. I won't pretend the way you handled the supplier money didn't hurt. I was angry for weeks. But I don't want to carry that into whatever comes next, so I'm putting it down here. I won't speak badly of you to customers or suppliers. What I'm keeping is the lesson: from now on, every partnership I enter gets written down on day one. I hope the van does well.

Rajni

qa.q: Which things does Rajni keep in the split?
qa.a: Rajni keeps the shop lease and the recipes.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel about what happened, and what does Rajni choose to do with it?
qa.a: Rajni is still hurt and was angry for weeks, but chooses not to carry it forward and not to speak badly of Vishal.

qa.q: What lesson is Rajni keeping, and how would it help in the next partnership?
qa.a: Rajni will write every partnership down on day one, so the terms and expectations are clear from the start.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vishal may feel relieved that the terms are clear and there is no attack, though possibly ashamed or uneasy since Rajni names the hurt directly.

grounding: Shows someone ending a partnership with clear terms, releasing bitterness and keeping the lesson.

passage: Varun stared at the email from the school group: they had gone with the other company. Nitin's team, the one Varun had privately called "the flashy ones," had won it. His first reaction was a hot, tight feeling in his chest. He closed the laptop, walked to the stairwell of the office in Pune and came back with a different question. Could he ask the school group why? He called and asked politely. The answer surprised him: Nitin's team had run the demo on the school group's own sample data and replied to every question the same day. Varun pulled the team together that afternoon. "Next demo, we use their data. And nobody leaves a question overnight." At the industry meet the next month, he walked over and congratulated Nitin.

qa.q: What did the school group say Nitin's team did differently in the demo?
qa.a: Nitin's team ran the demo on the school group's own sample data and answered every question the same day.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when the email arrived, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: He felt a hot, tight sting in his chest, then steadied himself and turned it into curiosity, calling the client to ask why they had chosen the other company.

qa.q: What did Varun change after learning why he lost?
qa.a: He decided future demos would use the client's own data and that no question would wait overnight. 👍

qa.q: How might Nitin see Varun's congratulations at the meet?
qa.a: Nitin may be a little surprised and see it as a sign of respect from a rival, though Nitin might still stay watchful.

grounding: Shows a salesperson studying why a rival won a deal, improving his own offering and treating the competitor as a teacher.

passage:
Friday night. Three days since Vinita's catering got the office canteen contract, and I've barely thought about anything else. I told two other stall owners her food is bland. I sent a long message to the market group about "people who undercut everyone." Today I felt good about it for about an hour. Then I saw a missed call from Mrs. Kulkarni, who orders for her daughter's engagement. She'd called twice. I never called back because I was busy checking Vinita's page for reviews. I feel a bit sick. The contract is gone, and now maybe the engagement order too. Tomorrow: call Mrs. Kulkarni first thing. I still don't like Vinita, but she's not the one losing my customers.

Rafiq

qa.q: Which contract did Vinita's catering win?
qa.a: Vinita's catering won the office canteen contract.

qa.q: What is Rafiq feeling toward Vinita, and what does the entry show it has cost him?
qa.a: Rafiq feels bitter and preoccupied, and the obsession cost a missed customer call because Rafiq was busy checking Vinita's reviews.

qa.q: What should Rafiq put his energy into instead of watching Vinita?
qa.a: Call Mrs. Kulkarni back first and give Rafiq's own customers full attention, and maybe learn honestly why the canteen chose Vinita.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Kulkarni have felt when her two calls went unanswered?
qa.a: She may have felt ignored and worried about the engagement order, and might start looking for another caterer.

grounding: Shows a business owner consumed by hatred of a rival who spreads negativity and neglects the business's own customers.

passage: The whole field smelled of fresh cut millet when Raghav looked up and saw his little son Hemant, three years old, running toward the pond behind the field. Raghav's heart slammed. He dropped the sickle, sprinted, and caught Hemant by the arm at the edge, shouting louder than he meant to. Hemant burst into tears. Raghav's hands were still shaking. He crouched in the mud. "I'm sorry I shouted. I was scared. I love you very much." Then, holding Hemant's hand, he walked him to a dry spot a few steps back. "We look at the frogs from here. Close to Papa." Hemant sniffled, pointed at a frog, and leaned his head against his father's arm.

qa.q: Where was Hemant running when Raghav saw him?
qa.a: Hemant was running toward the pond behind the field.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he shouted, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Raghav felt a sharp mix of fear and love, shown by his slamming heart, his shaking hands and how quickly he ran.

qa.q: How did Raghav repair the moment after losing his patience?
qa.a: He crouched down, apologised for shouting, said he had been scared and loved Hemant, then gave him a safe place to watch the frogs. 🤍

qa.q: What was that moment like for Hemant?
qa.a: Hemant was startled and frightened by the shout, then comforted by the apology and the closeness, as leaning on his father's arm suggests.

grounding: Shows a young father feeling love and fear together, guiding his child to safety and repairing after shouting.

passage: "Look what you've done! Every single morning!" Zeenat heard her own voice bounce off the kitchen tiles. The milk was spreading across the table, the school bus was due in ten minutes, and five-year-old Dilnaz stood frozen with her lip trembling. Zeenat's chest went hot with guilt at once. She stepped to the sink, ran the tap and took three slow breaths. Then she came back and crouched down. "Mummy shouted, and I'm sorry. Spilled milk is not a big problem. I was rushing and I got cross." Dilnaz sniffed. "Let's wipe it together," Zeenat said, handing her a cloth. They made the bus with a minute to spare, and Dilnaz waved from the window.

qa.q: What had Dilnaz spilled?
qa.a: Dilnaz spilled the milk on the table.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling right after she snapped?
qa.a: She felt hot guilt straight away, on top of stress about the bus, so she stopped at the sink to breathe.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do that teaches Dilnaz more than never getting angry would?
qa.a: She calmed herself, apologised, named her own mistake and cleaned up together, showing that anger can be mended.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt when her mother shouted, and afterwards?
qa.a: Dilnaz was probably scared and ashamed, as her frozen stance and trembling lip suggest, and then relieved when her mother came back kind. 🙂

grounding: Shows a parent snapping at her child, feeling guilty, then apologising and regulating herself.

passage: The power went out at five, in the middle of the storm, an hour before the prayers for Thakuma. Anirban stood in the dark hall with a candle and felt nothing at all, which frightened him more than tears would have. Then, suddenly, anger at the rain, at the neighbours who couldn't come, at the missed call from Sunday that he never returned. Underneath was a small flicker of relief that her long illness was over, and right behind it, guilt for feeling it. His friend Jeevan had waded through the flooded lane and now sat beside him without speaking. Anirban lit the lamp, did the rituals by candlelight, and let the tears come or not. When Jeevan finally said, "You can feel all of it," he nodded.

qa.q: What went out during the storm?
qa.a: The power went out at five, during the storm.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Anirban have, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt numb, then angry, guilty about the missed call and a little relieved, and he felt guilty about the relief. His fright at feeling nothing shows the numbness.

qa.q: What could Anirban do in the coming weeks to look after himself?
qa.a: Keep the rituals that comfort him, stay close to people like Jeevan, let each feeling come at its own pace, and see a counsellor if the heaviness does not ease. 🤍

qa.q: How might Jeevan have seen Anirban's silence that evening?
qa.a: Jeevan probably saw a friend in pain and chose to sit quietly without asking him to cry or explain.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving a grandmother with numbness, anger, guilt and relief, keeping rituals despite a storm and accepting support.

passage: By the second evening the courtyard of the old house was full of relatives and the smell of incense. Siddharth cried openly on the charpai, his face in his hands. His brother Pradeep hadn't stopped moving: chairs, tea, the cooking fire, a phone call about the priest. Bua leaned toward another aunt. "Pradeep hasn't shed a single tear." Siddharth heard it. "He's carrying the chairs," he said quietly. "That's how he does it. I do it this way." Late that night, Pradeep finally sat down next to him. "I keep thinking if I stop, I'll fall," he said. Siddharth passed him a glass of tea and stayed beside him until the lamp burned low.

qa.q: What was Pradeep doing while Siddharth was crying?
qa.a: Pradeep kept moving: chairs, tea, the cooking fire and a phone call about the priest.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep keep busy all day?
qa.a: He was afraid that if he stopped he would fall apart, as he tells Siddharth late at night.

qa.q: How could the relatives support both brothers instead of judging them?
qa.a: They could accept that crying and staying busy are both ways of grieving, give Pradeep a place to rest and sit with Siddharth.

qa.q: How might Bua's remark have felt to Pradeep if he had heard it?
qa.a: He might have felt judged and misunderstood, as if his grief did not count, when he was actually holding himself together.

grounding: Shows two brothers in a village mourning in different ways and supporting each other instead of judging.
